about: FFSA inspection checklist as used in the FFSA Fleet app (config/checklist), with every point's help text. checks: which inspection types include the point (pre, post, weekly, monthly, workshop). A monthly check covers every point tagged weekly OR monthly. measure: {u: unit, w: warn below, f: fail below} graded automatically.

checkTypes.label: Pre-trip check
checkTypes.desc: Quick go/no-go before the vehicle leaves
checkTypes.help: A few go/no-go points before the vehicle leaves. Any driver can do it in two minutes.

checkTypes.label: Post-trip check
checkTypes.desc: When the vehicle comes back: damage, km, fuel and anything the driver reports
checkTypes.help: When the vehicle comes back: new damage, km, fuel, cleanliness and anything the driver reports.

checkTypes.label: Weekly check
checkTypes.desc: Everything you can check without tools, on the vehicle’s inspection day
checkTypes.help: Everything you can check by looking, listening and driving, on the vehicle’s inspection day.

checkTypes.label: Monthly check
checkTypes.desc: The weekly points plus the once-a-month points, on the first inspection day of the month
checkTypes.help: The weekly points plus the slower once-a-month points. Done instead of the weekly check on the vehicle’s first inspection day of each month.

checkTypes.label: Workshop report
checkTypes.desc: Record the mechanic’s findings and attach their report
checkTypes.help: Points only a mechanic can check. Record them from the workshop’s report and attach it.

route.title: Get ready
route.instructions: Park on level ground, out of traffic. Engine off, handbrake on, keys in your pocket. Ideally the engine has been off for an hour, so it’s cold. Bring: a tread depth gauge, a tyre pressure gauge, a torch, a cloth or paper towel, and your phone for photos. A helper makes the lights check much easier.

route.title: Under the bonnet
route.instructions: Engine off and cold. Open the bonnet with the release lever inside the cab, then the safety catch under the front edge. Prop it up properly before you lean in.

route.title: Walk around the outside
route.instructions: Start at the front and walk clockwise all the way round. Take the six walk-around photos as you go: the same angles every time.

route.title: Tyres and wheels
route.instructions: Go round each wheel in turn: front left, front right, rear right, rear left, then the spare.

route.title: Inside, engine off
route.instructions: Open every door and check every seat.

route.title: Engine running, standing still
route.instructions: Sit in the driver’s seat, foot on the brake, gear in P (or neutral with the handbrake on), and start the engine.

route.title: Lights
route.instructions: Ask a helper to stand in front, then behind, while you switch each light on. Alone? Use the reflection in a window or wall at dusk.

route.title: Road test
route.instructions: Seat belt on. Use a quiet road you know, with no traffic behind you when you test the brakes. Radio off, windows slightly open, so you can hear.

route.title: From the workshop report
route.instructions: Copy what the mechanic’s report says for each point, and attach the report.

items.text: Driver reports no problems on the trip (noises, warning lights, handling)
items.hint: Ask the driver and note anything they mention

help.why: The driver knows better than anyone how the vehicle behaved on the trip. Small signs, like a new noise or a warning light that came on and went off, are often the first clue of a problem that is still cheap to fix.
howToCheck: Ask the driver: “Did anything feel, sound or smell different? Did any warning light come on? Did anything break or stop working?”
Ask about any bumps, kerbs, potholes or near-misses, even small ones.
Write down what they say, in their words, in the note.
help.markMonitor: Something small to keep an eye on, like a rattle or weak aircon.
help.markFixNow: A warning light, a brake or steering problem, overheating, or anything that made the vehicle feel unsafe.
help.looksLike: A good handover is a short chat at the vehicle, keys in hand, before the driver walks away.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Drivers often forget small things. Ask each question one by one rather than “All fine?”.

whatGoesWrong.problem: A warning light that came and went
whatGoesWrong.signs: Ask: “Did any light come on, even for a moment?” Lights that flicker on and off are still worth checking.
Ask about potholes, kerbs, gravel roads and parking. Then look at that corner of the vehicle yourself.

items.text: Keys, remote and locknut key returned

help.why: A lost key or remote costs a lot to replace and could let someone steal the vehicle. The locknut key is the special socket for the locking wheel nut: without it nobody can take a wheel off to change a flat tyre.
howToCheck: Count the keys and remotes handed back against what went out.
Press the remote buttons: it should lock and unlock from a few metres away.
Check the locknut key is in the vehicle (usually in the cubby hole or with the jack).
help.markMonitor: Remote only works close up: its battery is getting weak.
help.markFixNow: A key, remote or the locknut key is missing.
help.looksLike: Every key goes back on its own labelled hook or tag. The remote has buttons that press and spring back. The locknut key is a small, round socket with a pattern on its end, usually in a little bag.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Count them against what was handed out.
The remote only works when you stand right next to the vehicle, or you must press several times.
A bent blade, a cracked case or a loose button.

items.hint: Check the expiry date on the windscreen disc

help.why: The licence disc shows the vehicle is registered and its yearly licence fee is paid. Driving with an expired disc can get the driver fined and the vehicle stopped at a roadblock, and it can cause trouble with the insurance after an accident.
howToCheck: Find the disc on the inside of the windscreen, usually at the bottom left.
Read the expiry date.
Check the registration number on the disc matches the number plate.
Make sure it’s easy to read from outside and not faded or covered.
help.markOk: Valid for more than a month.
help.markMonitor: Expires within the next month: renew it now.
help.markFixNow: Expired, missing, or belongs to another vehicle.
help.looksLike: A round paper disc, about the size of a coaster, in a clear holder on the inside of the windscreen, usually at the bottom left as you sit in the driver’s seat. It shows the registration number, the VIN, the engine number and the expiry date.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The expiry date has passed.
The registration number on the disc doesn’t match the number plate.
Faded by the sun, wet, or the holder has fallen off.
The holder is empty. A new disc may be in the office and not yet fitted.

items.text: Copy of registration papers in the vehicle

help.why: Traffic officers can ask for proof of who owns the vehicle, and border posts ask for it on trips outside South Africa. A copy in the vehicle saves a lot of trouble. Keep the original safe in the office.
howToCheck: Look in the cubby hole or document wallet for a copy of the registration certificate.
Check it’s for this vehicle: the registration number and VIN must match.
Before a trip outside South Africa, also check the permission letter and other border papers are there.
help.markFixNow: No copy, or another vehicle’s papers.

items.text: Insurance and roadside-assistance numbers in the vehicle

help.why: After an accident or breakdown, the driver needs to phone the insurer or roadside assistance quickly, often while stressed. If the numbers are already in the vehicle, help comes faster.
howToCheck: Look for the insurance card or sticker with the policy number, the claims number and the roadside assistance number.
Check the numbers are current.
help.markOk: Card is there and the numbers are current.
help.markMonitor: Card is old or hard to read.
help.markFixNow: No insurance or roadside numbers in the vehicle.

items.text: Service book or service history up to date

help.why: The service book proves the vehicle has been looked after. It tells the workshop what was done last time and makes the vehicle worth more when it’s sold. WeBuyCars marked the Kombi’s service history as “no record”, which pushed its offer down.
howToCheck: Find the service book (in the cubby hole or the office file).
Look at the last stamp: date, km and workshop.
Compare it with the last service in this app.
At a workshop visit: take the service book along and ask the workshop to stamp it with the date, km and work done.
help.markOk: Last service is stamped and matches the app.
help.markMonitor: Stamp missing, but there’s an invoice for the service.
help.markFixNow: No service book or service history at all.
help.looksLike: The service book is a small booklet with a page for each service. Each page has the date, the km, the work done and the workshop’s stamp. Some vehicles have invoices in a file instead.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A service happened (there’s an invoice) but the book wasn’t stamped.
A long time or many km between two stamps.
Nobody knows where it is: check the office file and the cubby hole.

help.why: If the only key is lost or breaks, the vehicle can’t be used until a new one is made, which can take days and cost thousands of rands. A spare key kept safely means the vehicle keeps working.
howToCheck: Check the spare key is in the key safe or office.
Try it in the door lock now and then so you know it still works.
help.markMonitor: Spare is there, but its remote battery is flat.
help.markFixNow: No spare key.
help.looksLike: The spare key is kept in the office key safe, not in the vehicle. It should look like the main key and open the vehicle.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It isn’t in the key safe.
It won’t turn in the door lock or start the vehicle.
The spare’s remote doesn’t lock or unlock the doors.

items.hint: Not checked for now: there’s no way to check it yet

help.why: The tracking unit lets the tracking company find the vehicle if it’s stolen, and the insurer may require one. The immobiliser stops the engine starting without the right key. If either one fails, a stolen vehicle may never be found.
howToCheck: Check the tracking company’s app or website shows the vehicle’s current location.
Look for a tracker warning light or message on the dashboard.
Not sure? Phone the tracking company and ask them to test the unit.
help.markOk: Shows the right location, no warnings.
help.markFixNow: Not reporting at all, or the tracking company says it’s faulty.
help.looksLike: The tracking unit is hidden inside the vehicle, so you check it through the tracking company’s app or website, which should show the vehicle on a map where it really is.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The map shows an old location or an old date and time.
Loose wires under the dashboard, or a fuse missing.
The vehicle won’t start with the right key, or a security light keeps flashing.

items.text: Walk-around: any new dents, scratches or damage

help.why: Walking around the vehicle before and after every trip shows whether new damage happened during that trip. That tells FFSA who is responsible and stops damage being blamed on the wrong person. A photo is the best proof.
howToCheck: Walk slowly all the way round, about one big step away from the vehicle.
Look at every panel, bumper, light and mirror for new dents, scratches or cracks. Crouch down to see the lower parts.
Compare with the photos from the last check.
Photograph anything new close up, and once from further away so it’s clear where it is.
help.markMonitor: A new small scratch or stone chip.
help.markFixNow: A new dent, crack, broken light or mirror, or any damage that makes it unsafe.
help.looksLike: Paint should look smooth with an even shine. Panels should line up with even gaps between them, about the width of a finger. Every light, mirror and badge should be in place.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Look along the panel at an angle with the light behind you: a dent makes the reflection bend or wobble.
A bright line, or a line of different colour, on the paint. Run a fingernail across it: if the nail catches, it’s deep.
Grey or black marks and scraped paint on bumper corners, from parking.
Cracks in lights, mirror covers or bumpers, or pieces missing.

help.why: The front bumper and grille take the most stone chips and knocks. A loose bumper can fall off at speed, and a broken grille lets stones hit the radiator, which cools the engine.
howToCheck: Look for cracks, dents and scrapes.
Gently push and pull the bumper. It shouldn’t move or rattle.
Look through the grille for damage behind it.
help.markFixNow: Loose, hanging, or sharp broken edges.
help.looksLike: The front bumper is the big plastic part below the headlights. It should sit flush, with even gaps to the headlights and wings. The grille (the slatted part in the middle) should be complete.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A gap that is wider on one side, or the bumper moves when you push it gently.
Thin lines in the paint, often around old repairs.
The bumper edge sticks out near the wheel arch.
Missing slats, or holes where stones went through.

help.why: The rear bumper protects the back of the vehicle in parking knocks and holds the number plate, and often the parking sensors and some lights.
howToCheck: Look for cracks, dents and scrapes.
Push and pull it gently. It shouldn’t move.
Check the clips at the corners are holding it in place.
help.markMonitor: New scrapes, or a corner clip loose.
help.markFixNow: Hanging, badly cracked or sharp edges.
help.looksLike: The rear bumper wraps around the back of the vehicle under the tailgate or boot. It should sit flush with even gaps to the body and lights.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A corner drops away from the body, often from broken clips.
Scuffs, scrapes or dents at the corners.
Small round parking sensors pushed in, cracked or missing.

help.why: The bonnet covers the engine. If its catch is damaged, it can fly open while driving and block the driver’s view completely.
howToCheck: Look for dents and stone chips.
Close it firmly, then try to lift the front edge with your fingers. It must not lift.
help.markFixNow: Doesn’t latch, or lifts when you pull it.
help.looksLike: The bonnet should sit level, with the same gap on both sides, and line up with the wings and headlights.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Small white or dark dots on the front edge, where paint has chipped off.
One side sits higher, or the edge lifts when you pull on it.
Wobbly reflections across the top.

help.why: Side panels and doors protect passengers in a side crash. Doors must open and close properly so people can get in and out, and get out fast in an emergency.
howToCheck: Stand at the front corner and look along the side with the light behind you. Dents show up as wobbly reflections.
Open and close each door. It should close with one firm push and not rattle.
Check the door handles work inside and out.
help.markFixNow: A door won’t open, close or lock properly, or damage with sharp edges.
help.looksLike: The left side: front wing, doors, sliding door or rear doors, and the rear quarter panel behind the back wheel. Doors should close flush with the body and with even gaps.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Small round dents at about knee to waist height, from other car doors.
A scratch along several panels, from a pole, wall or another vehicle.
The door sticks out at one edge, or needs a hard slam to close.

help.why: Side panels and doors protect passengers in a side crash. Doors must open and close properly so people can get in and out, and get out fast in an emergency.
howToCheck: Stand at the front corner and look along the side with the light behind you. Dents show up as wobbly reflections.
Open and close each door. It should close with one firm push and not rattle.
Check the door handles work inside and out.
help.markFixNow: A door won’t open, close or lock properly, or damage with sharp edges.
help.looksLike: The right side: front wing, doors, and the rear quarter panel behind the back wheel. Doors should close flush with the body and with even gaps.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Small round dents at about knee to waist height, from other car doors.
A scratch along several panels, from a pole, wall or another vehicle.
The door sticks out at one edge, or needs a hard slam to close.

help.why: Damage on the roof is easy to miss. Blocked gutters cause rust and leaks, and a loose roof rack or load can fall off on the highway onto the car behind.
howToCheck: Look from a step, a ladder or a higher spot.
Check for dents, rust, and leaves or dirt in the gutters along the edges.
If there’s a roof rack, shake it. It must be solid with no loose bolts.
help.markFixNow: Loose roof rack, or a hole or rust through the metal.
help.looksLike: The roof should be smooth and evenly coloured. The gutters (the channels along the edges of the roof) should be clear. A roof rack should be bolted down tight with no rust around its feet.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Lots of small round dents, easiest to see with the light low.
Leaves, sand or dirt in the channels.
It moves or creaks when you push it.
Orange-brown spots or bubbled paint around the rack feet or the edges.

items.text: Sliding door runs, latches and locks

help.why: Vans have heavy sliding doors that get used all day. If the runner or latch wears out, the door can jam, come off its track, or slide open while driving, which is dangerous for passengers.
howToCheck: Open the sliding door all the way. It should click and stay open by itself.
Close it. It should run smoothly and lock with one firm push.
Look at the runner (the track along the side of the van) for dirt or damage.
Check the door also opens from the inside.
help.markMonitor: Stiff or noisy: needs cleaning and grease.
help.markFixNow: Jams, comes off the track, won’t lock, or won’t stay open. Mark N/A on cars without a sliding door.
help.looksLike: A sliding door runs on rails: one at the top, one at the bottom (inside the step area) and one along the side of the vehicle at the back. The rails should be clean, the door should slide freely, and it should lock open at the end with a click.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Sand or grit in the lower rail; the door feels gritty or noisy.
The door drops when you open it, scrapes the body, or won’t latch.
It rolls back on a slope: dangerous for fingers.
The dashboard says a door is open when it isn’t: a sensor or latch fault.

items.text: Tailgate or boot opens, closes and locks

help.why: A boot or tailgate that doesn’t lock lets luggage get stolen or fall out on the road. A tailgate that won’t stay up can fall on someone’s head. (The CR-V’s tailgate doesn’t close properly.)
howToCheck: Open the tailgate fully. It must stay up by itself.
Close it and pull on it to check it’s locked.
Lock the vehicle with the remote and check the tailgate locks too.
help.markOk: Opens, stays up, closes and locks.
help.markMonitor: Needs a hard slam to close, or drops slowly.
help.markFixNow: Won’t lock, won’t stay closed, or won’t stay up.
help.looksLike: The tailgate or boot lid should open with the handle or button, rise and stay up by itself (held by gas struts, the shiny rods at the sides), and close and lock with one firm push.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The tailgate drifts down or drops on its own.
It needs a hard slam, or springs open again.
The handle moves but nothing happens.
It stays unlocked when the rest of the vehicle locks.

help.why: A missing or loose fuel cap lets fuel smell and fumes out and dirt and water in, and can switch on the engine warning light.
howToCheck: Open the fuel flap and check the cap is there.
Turn the cap until it clicks.
help.markMonitor: Cap is damaged but still closes.
help.markFixNow: Cap missing.
help.looksLike: Behind a small flap on the side of the vehicle. The cap should be there, with its rubber seal intact, and click when tightened. Tip: the little arrow next to the fuel pump symbol on the fuel gauge shows which side the flap is on.

whatGoesWrong.signs: An open filler neck, or a temporary cap.
It turns without clicking, or comes off easily.
A strong smell of diesel or petrol near the flap.

items.text: Number plates secure and readable, front and rear

help.why: Number plates must be easy to read so the vehicle can be identified. Missing, cracked or unreadable plates get fines and get the vehicle stopped. Toll gates and speed cameras also need to read them.
howToCheck: Check the front and back plates are firmly fixed and not cracked.
Stand about 20 m away and try to read them.
Wipe them clean if they’re dirty.
help.markFixNow: Missing, loose, or can’t be read.
help.looksLike: Reflective plates with black letters and the province strip, bolted or riveted on firmly at the front and back. All letters must be clear.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It rattles, hangs at an angle, or is gone.
Cracks through the letters, or letters you can’t read from 20 m.
Mud over the letters, common after gravel roads.

items.text: Rust on sills, wheel arches or door bottoms

help.why: Rust eats metal from the inside out. Small rust spots are cheap to fix, but left alone they spread, weaken the body, and can make the vehicle fail a roadworthy test.
howToCheck: Look at the bottom edges of the doors, the sills (the strip under the doors) and around the wheel arches.
Look for orange-brown spots or paint that is bubbling up.
Photograph any rust so you can see if it grows.
help.markMonitor: Small surface spots or bubbling paint.
help.markFixNow: Holes, or rust flaking through the metal.
help.looksLike: Look low down: the sills (the strip under the doors), the bottom edges of the doors, and around the wheel arches. Paint here should be smooth and the same colour as the rest of the vehicle.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Small orange-brown spots.
Little blisters in the paint. Rust is growing underneath.
Flaking metal or holes. This fails a roadworthy test.

help.why: The rubbers around the doors and windows keep rain and dust out. A torn seal causes leaks, wet carpets that smell and rust, and wind noise.
howToCheck: Look at the rubber around each door and the tailgate for tears or loose pieces.
After rain, feel the carpets for damp patches.
help.markMonitor: Small tear or a loose section.
help.markFixNow: Water getting inside.
help.looksLike: Black rubber strips around every door, window and the tailgate. They should be soft, unbroken and pressed firmly into place.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Splits or missing pieces, often at the bottom corners.
A loop of rubber hanging out of the door frame.
Damp carpets, a musty smell, or water marks after rain.

items.text: Tow bar and trailer socket (if fitted)

help.why: A tow bar pulls a trailer. If it’s loose, the trailer can break free. If the trailer socket doesn’t work, the trailer’s lights don’t work and nobody behind can see it braking or turning.
howToCheck: Shake the tow ball firmly. It must not move.
Check the bolts and the safety chain point aren’t damaged or rusted through.
When a trailer is hooked up, check its brake lights and indicators work.
help.markFixNow: Loose tow ball, or the socket doesn’t work. Mark N/A if there’s no tow bar.
help.looksLike: A metal ball on a bracket under the back bumper, with a round electrical socket next to it. The ball should be rigid and the socket cover should close.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It moves when you shake it hard.
Green or white powder inside the socket; trailer lights don’t work.
The ball sits crooked.

items.text: Windscreen free of cracks and chips
items.hint: A crack in the driver’s line of sight fails a roadworthy test

help.why: The driver has to see clearly. A small chip can turn into a long crack when the vehicle hits a bump or the sun heats the glass. A crack in front of the driver fails a roadworthy test, and a cracked windscreen is weaker in a crash.
howToCheck: Stand in front and look at the windscreen at an angle; chips show up better that way.
Then sit in the driver’s seat and look out.
Note where any chips or cracks are. The area the driver’s wiper cleans matters most.
help.markMonitor: A small chip outside the driver’s view: get it repaired soon, it’s cheap.
help.markFixNow: Any crack, or a chip in the driver’s view.
help.looksLike: The windscreen should be clear glass with no marks in front of the driver. A chip looks like a tiny star or bullseye; a crack is a line that may grow.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A small star or bullseye, easiest to see from outside at an angle.
A line, often starting from a chip or the edge of the glass.
Curved scratch lines across the glass from worn blades.
The glass looks hazy or glary when you drive into the sun.

help.why: Side and rear windows let the driver see around the vehicle and keep passengers safe and dry.
howToCheck: Look at each window for cracks and chips.
Check window tint isn’t peeling so badly that it blocks the view.
help.markFixNow: A cracked or broken window.
help.looksLike: All side and back windows should be clear and complete. Window tint should be smooth with no bubbles over the driver’s view.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Lines or chips in the glass.
Glass missing or covered with plastic: a security risk.
Bubbles or loose film, especially on the driver’s window.

help.why: Windows must open in an emergency, and close to keep rain and thieves out. A window stuck open is a security risk when the vehicle is parked overnight.
howToCheck: Open and close each window with its switch.
It should move smoothly and close all the way.
help.markFixNow: A window won’t close.
help.looksLike: With the ignition on, each window should go all the way down and all the way up smoothly in a few seconds, and stop by itself at the top.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The motor or the rails are wearing out.
The glass slides down on its own or goes up crooked: a broken regulator.
Nothing happens from one switch, but the window works from the driver’s switch.

items.text: Side mirrors secure, glass intact, adjust properly

help.why: Mirrors show the driver what’s beside and behind the vehicle, especially when changing lanes. Vans are big with large blind spots, so good mirrors prevent side-swipes.
howToCheck: Check both side mirrors are firmly attached and the glass isn’t cracked.
Sit in the driver’s seat and adjust them. You should just see the side of the vehicle and the lane next to you.
help.markMonitor: Glass slightly cracked, or adjuster stiff.
help.markFixNow: Mirror missing, loose, or glass broken.
help.looksLike: Both side mirrors fixed firmly to the doors, the glass complete with no cracks, and the mirrors can be adjusted so the driver sees the lane beside the vehicle.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Lines across the mirror; the view is broken up.
It flops when you touch it or shakes while driving.
The coloured cover on the back is gone.
The mirror won’t move with the switch or by hand.

help.why: The inside mirror shows what’s behind the vehicle. It must be secure and adjustable, even if luggage sometimes blocks the view.
howToCheck: Check it’s firmly attached and the glass is clear.
Adjust it to see out of the back window.
help.markFixNow: Missing or broken.
help.looksLike: The inside mirror is fixed to the windscreen or roof. It should be firm, the glass clear, and the driver should be able to see out of the back window.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It droops or wobbles while driving.
The mount has come away from the windscreen.

items.text: Wiper blades not split or smearing

help.why: Wiper blades clear rain from the windscreen. The sun makes the rubber hard and cracked, so it leaves streaks, which makes it hard to see in a storm, especially at night.
howToCheck: Lift each wiper arm and run a finger along the rubber. It should be soft and smooth, not cracked or torn.
Spray washer fluid and switch on the wipers. They should clean the glass in one sweep without streaks or juddering.
help.markFixNow: Rubber torn or hanging off.
help.looksLike: Each blade is a thin strip of rubber on a metal or plastic arm. The rubber edge should be straight, soft and smooth, with no cracks or tears.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Run a finger along the edge: it feels rough or crumbly.
A piece of rubber hanging loose.
Lines of water left behind after a wipe.
The blade jumps and chatters across the glass.

help.why: In heavy rain the wipers must be fast enough to keep the windscreen clear.
howToCheck: Wet the windscreen with washer fluid.
Try every wiper speed, including the slow on-and-off setting.
They should move smoothly and stop at the bottom of the windscreen.
help.markFixNow: Wipers don’t work.
help.looksLike: The wiper stalk is on the steering column. Its settings are: off, intermittent (on-and-off), slow, fast, and one quick wipe. The wipers should sweep smoothly and park at the bottom of the windscreen.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Blown fuse or a failed motor.
One setting does nothing.
They don’t park at the bottom when switched off.

items.text: Washer jets spray onto the windscreen

help.why: Washer spray clears dust, mud and squashed insects. On a dusty road with the sun low, a dirty windscreen can blind the driver.
howToCheck: Pull the washer lever.
Spray from each jet should land on the middle of the windscreen.
help.markMonitor: Weak spray, or a jet aims too high or low.
help.markFixNow: Nothing comes out.
help.looksLike: Pull the wiper stalk towards you to spray. The jets are small nozzles on the bonnet or under the wiper arms. The spray should hit the middle of the windscreen.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The tank is empty, or the pump has failed (listen for a buzz).
One jet sprays weakly or not at all.
The spray goes over the roof or hits the bottom of the glass.

help.why: Lights let the driver see at night and let others see the vehicle and know when it’s braking or turning. This quick check prevents many accidents.
howToCheck: Switch on the headlights and walk round to see they work.
Switch on the hazard lights: every indicator should flash.
Ask someone to watch while you press the brake pedal, or reverse close to a wall and look in the mirror for the red glow.
help.markMonitor: A small light out, like the number plate light.
help.markFixNow: A headlight, brake light or indicator doesn’t work.
help.looksLike: Every light should light up clearly and evenly. Indicators should flash at a steady speed, roughly once a second.

whatGoesWrong.signs: One light is dark while its partner on the other side works.
Usually a blown indicator bulb on that side.
A dirty or yellowed lens, or a bad connection.

help.why: Dipped headlights are the normal night-driving lights. They light the road without blinding other drivers. With one out, the vehicle can look like a motorbike to oncoming drivers.
howToCheck: Switch on the headlights (dipped).
Stand in front: both must work and be equally bright.
Against a wall, check they point down, not up into other drivers’ eyes.
help.markMonitor: One is dimmer than the other.
help.markFixNow: One or both don’t work.
help.looksLike: Two headlights on the normal setting light the road ahead and slightly to the left, with a clear cut-off line at the top.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Only one side lights the road.
Oncoming cars flash their lights at you.
Fog or droplets inside the headlight.

help.why: Bright lights light the road far ahead on dark country roads, so the driver sees animals and people sooner.
howToCheck: Switch to bright (push or pull the indicator stalk).
Both headlights should get brighter and the blue light on the dashboard should come on.
help.markFixNow: Brights don’t work.
help.looksLike: Brights light the road much further ahead. A blue headlight symbol shows on the dashboard.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The beam doesn’t get stronger and the blue light doesn’t show.
Only one headlight brightens.

items.text: Park lights and daytime running lights

help.why: Park lights and daytime running lights make the vehicle easier to see, for example when it’s parked on the side of the road at dusk.
howToCheck: Switch to the park-light position and walk around. The small front and rear lights should be on.
help.markFixNow: None work.
help.looksLike: Small white or amber lights at the front corners and red lights at the back, on whenever the light switch is on. Some vehicles also have daytime running lights.

whatGoesWrong.signs: One corner is dark.
None of the park lights work: a fuse or a switch fault.

help.why: Indicators tell other drivers that you’re turning or changing lanes. Without them, other drivers can’t guess what you’ll do.
howToCheck: Switch on the left indicator and walk around: the front, side and rear lights on that side should flash.
Repeat on the right.
If an indicator flashes very fast, a bulb is usually blown.
help.markFixNow: A front or rear indicator doesn’t work.
help.looksLike: Amber lights at the front, on the sides (on the wings or mirrors) and at the back. They flash about once a second, with a ticking sound and a green arrow on the dashboard.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The indicator on that side flashes fast or stays on without flashing.
The small light on the wing or mirror is cracked or dark.
The amber colour is weak in daylight.

help.why: Hazard lights warn others when the vehicle is stopped in a dangerous place, like after a breakdown.
howToCheck: Press the hazard button (the red triangle).
All the indicators should flash together.
help.markFixNow: Don’t work.
help.looksLike: The hazard button has a red triangle on it, usually in the middle of the dashboard. All the indicators flash together.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Nothing flashes, or only some lights flash.
The hazards won’t switch off.

items.text: Brake lights, including the high third light
items.hint: Ask someone to stand behind the vehicle

help.why: Brake lights tell the driver behind that you’re slowing down. If they don’t work, you can be hit from behind.
howToCheck: Ask someone to stand behind while you press the brake pedal.
Both brake lights and the high third light must come on.
Alone? At dusk, reverse close to a wall or window and look in the mirror for the red glow when you press the brake.
help.markMonitor: Only the high third light is out.
help.markFixNow: A main brake light doesn’t work.
help.looksLike: Two bright red lights at the back, plus a high third light at the top of the back window or tailgate. They come on only while the brake pedal is pressed and are brighter than the tail lights.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A blown bulb.
A failed brake light switch at the pedal, or a fuse.
The high light doesn’t come on.
They stay on when you’re not braking.

help.why: Tail lights show the back of the vehicle at night so others don’t drive into it.
howToCheck: Switch on the lights and check both rear lights glow red.
help.markFixNow: One or both don’t work.
help.looksLike: Two red lights at the back that come on with the headlights. They are dimmer than the brake lights.

whatGoesWrong.signs: One side is dark at night.
White light shows through a crack.

help.why: Reverse lights warn people behind that the vehicle is about to reverse, and help the driver see behind at night.
help.safetyFirst: Keep your foot on the brake while you do this.
howToCheck: Start the engine. With your foot on the brake (and the handbrake on), select reverse.
Check the white lights at the back come on (ask a helper, or look in a window reflection).
help.markFixNow: Neither works.
help.looksLike: White lights at the back that come on only when reverse is selected.

whatGoesWrong.signs: No white light in reverse.
A switch fault on the gearbox.

help.why: The back number plate must be readable at night. A missing plate light can get a fine.
howToCheck: Switch on the lights and check the small light above the back plate works.
help.looksLike: One or two small white lights above the back number plate, lighting the plate at night.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The plate is dark at night.
Rust or water inside the small cover.

help.why: Fog lights help others see the vehicle, and help the driver see the road edge, in thick mist.
howToCheck: Switch on the fog lights and check the front ones (and the rear one, if there is one).
help.markFixNow: Mark N/A if there are no fog lights.
help.looksLike: Small lights low in the front bumper, and sometimes one bright red light at the back, switched on separately. A fog light symbol shows on the dashboard.

whatGoesWrong.signs: One side is dark.
Cracked or stone-damaged glass, low in the bumper.

items.text: Headlight lenses clear, not cracked or yellowed

help.why: Cracked or yellowed headlight covers make the light weak and scattered, so the driver sees less at night. Water getting in through cracks also blows bulbs.
howToCheck: Look at each headlight and tail light cover for cracks, holes or water inside.
Look for a cloudy yellow colour on the headlights.
help.markFixNow: Cracked, or water inside.
help.looksLike: Headlight covers should be clear like glass, with no cracks, holes or water inside.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The plastic looks frosted; light at night is weak and scattered.
A crack or stone hole lets water in and blows bulbs.
Mist or droplets inside the light.

help.why: Inside lights help passengers get in and out safely at night and help find things that have been dropped.
howToCheck: Open each door: the inside light should come on.
Check the switches on the roof lights work.
help.looksLike: Roof lights inside the cabin and the load area. Each one usually has three settings: on, off, and on when a door opens.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A bulb or switch fault.
A door switch is stuck. This can flatten the battery overnight.

help.why: Reflectors bounce other cars’ headlights back, so the vehicle can be seen even when its own lights are off, for example when it’s broken down at night.
howToCheck: Find the red reflectors at the back (often built into the bumper or lights).
Check they’re clean and not broken.
help.markFixNow: Missing or broken.
help.looksLike: Red reflectors at the back (often built into the bumper or lights), and on vans sometimes reflective tape on the sides and back. They should be clean and complete.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A gap where the reflector should be.
It doesn’t shine when torchlight hits it.

items.text: Tyres look properly inflated, no visible damage

help.why: A soft or damaged tyre can burst at speed, which can make a vehicle roll, especially a loaded van. A 30-second look before leaving catches most problems.
howToCheck: Walk around and look at each tyre. Does one look flatter than the others?
Look for cuts, bulges or nails.
If one looks soft, check its pressure before you leave.
help.markMonitor: One looks a bit soft: check and pump it up.
help.markFixNow: A flat tyre, a bulge, or a deep cut.
help.looksLike: All four tyres should look the same: round at the bottom with a slight bulge where they touch the ground. The sides should be smooth, with no cuts or lumps.

whatGoesWrong.signs: One tyre bulges more at the bottom than the others.
A nail or screw head in the tread, or a hissing sound.
A round lump on the side of the tyre. Don’t drive on it.

items.hint: Legal minimum in South Africa is 1.6 mm

help.why: Tread is the pattern of grooves on the tyre. The grooves push water out from under the tyre so it can grip the road. With shallow grooves the vehicle can slide on a wet road, like running on a wet floor in shoes with smooth soles. In South Africa it’s illegal to drive on tyres with less than 1.6 mm of tread.
howToCheck: Use a tread depth gauge (a cheap tool from any tyre or parts shop).
Push the pin into the deepest groove near the middle of the tyre and read the number in mm.
Measure in two or three places around the tyre and type in the lowest number. The app marks OK, Monitor or Fix now for you.
No gauge? Look inside the grooves for small raised bars (wear indicators). If the tread is level with those bars, the tyre is down to 1.6 mm.
help.markMonitor: Between 1.6 and 3 mm: plan new tyres soon.
help.markFixNow: Under 1.6 mm, or any bald patch. It’s illegal and unsafe.
help.looksLike: New tread is about 8 mm deep. In the grooves there are small raised bars (wear indicators); when the tread is level with them, the tyre is down to 1.6 mm.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The gauge reads under 3 mm, or the tread is level with the wear bars.
One edge much lower than the other.

whatGoesWrong.problem: Stone or nail in the tread
whatGoesWrong.signs: Remove small stones; leave nails in and get the tyre repaired.
