help.why: A spare wheel is useless if it’s flat, worn out or missing when you get a puncture far from town.
howToCheck: Find the spare. On vans it usually hangs in a cradle under the vehicle; in cars it’s under the boot floor.
Check it’s there and has tread.
Check its pressure. Spares lose air slowly while they wait.
help.markFixNow: Missing, flat, or worn out.
help.looksLike: A full wheel and tyre, the same as the others or a thinner space-saver, held firmly in place with air in it.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Squeeze it, or check it with a pressure gauge: spares lose air slowly while they wait.
Low tread, or cracks in the rubber.
The carrier or well is empty.
On vans with the spare underneath, the lowering bolt or winch is rusted and won’t turn.

items.text: Tyre pressures set to the door-pillar sticker
items.hint: Check when the tyres are cold

help.why: The right air pressure lets tyres grip properly, wear evenly and use less fuel. A tyre with too little air gets hot and can burst, especially with a full van on the highway.
howToCheck: Check when the tyres are cold: before driving, or after the vehicle has stood for an hour.
Find the right pressures on the sticker on the driver’s door frame or inside the fuel flap. There are often two numbers: use the higher “full load” one when the van will be full.
Check each tyre with a pressure gauge (or the machine at a petrol station) and add air where needed.
Put the valve caps back on.
help.markMonitor: One was low but held after pumping it up.
help.markFixNow: A tyre keeps losing air (a slow puncture).
help.looksLike: The pressure sticker shows the right pressure for the front and the back tyres, often with a higher “full load” number. A pressure gauge reads in bar or kPa (2.2 bar is 220 kPa).

whatGoesWrong.signs: The gauge reads below the sticker.
The same tyre is low again a few days after pumping it up.
Hissing at the valve when you press it lightly, or a missing valve cap.

items.text: Sidewalls free of cuts, bulges and cracks

help.why: The sidewall is the side of the tyre. A bulge means the inside of the tyre is broken and it can burst at any moment. Cuts usually come from kerbs and potholes.
howToCheck: Look at the outside wall of every tyre.
Turn the steering wheel all the way to see the inside wall of the front tyres.
Look for bulges, cuts, cracks, or anything stuck in the tyre.
help.markFixNow: Any bulge, a deep cut, or cords showing.
help.looksLike: The sidewall is the smooth side of the tyre with the size and brand written on it. It should be smooth and evenly black.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A round lump: the inside of the tyre is broken. It can burst.
A slice in the rubber, often from a kerb or sharp stone.
Lots of fine cracks, a sign of an old tyre.
Scuffs where the tyre rubbed a kerb.

items.hint: Worn edges point to alignment or pressure problems

help.why: The way a tyre wears tells a story. Wear on one edge usually means the wheels are out of alignment. Wear on both edges means too little air. Wear in the middle means too much air. Fixing the cause early saves buying new tyres.
howToCheck: Look across each tyre and compare the inner edge, the middle and the outer edge.
If it looks uneven, measure the tread on each edge with the gauge.
help.markFixNow: One edge worn down to the wire.
help.looksLike: The tread should be about the same depth across the whole width of each tyre: inner edge, middle and outer edge.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Wheel alignment is out.
The tyre has been driven too soft.
The tyre has been pumped too hard.
Worn shock absorbers or suspension.

items.text: All wheel nuts present; locknut key in the vehicle

help.why: Wheel nuts hold the wheels on. A missing or loose nut puts more strain on the others, and in the worst case the wheel comes off. The locknut key is needed to undo the special locking nut.
howToCheck: Count the nuts on each wheel. None should be missing.
Look for rust streaks coming from a nut, which can mean it’s loose.
Check the locknut key is in the vehicle.
help.markOk: All there, key in the vehicle.
help.markMonitor: A rust streak: ask the workshop to check the torque.
help.markFixNow: A missing nut, or no locknut key.
help.looksLike: Each wheel has the same number of shiny nuts or bolts in a circle (usually 5 or 6). One per wheel may be a special locking nut with a pattern on its face.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A gap in the circle of nuts.
A rust-coloured streak running out from a nut.
The pattern on the locking nut is chewed, so the key won’t fit.

items.text: Rims free of cracks and bends

help.why: A bent or cracked rim can let air leak out slowly, or break when the vehicle hits a pothole.
howToCheck: Look at each rim for cracks, missing chunks or bent edges.
A shaking steering wheel after hitting a pothole can mean a bent rim.
help.markFixNow: Cracked or bent.
help.looksLike: The rim is the metal wheel. Its edge should be round and smooth, with no cracks or missing pieces.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A flat spot or dent on the edge; the steering wheel shakes at speed.
A fine line, often near the spokes or the edge. A slow leak is common.
Scraped or chipped edges.

items.hint: 4-digit date code on the sidewall: 2321 = week 23 of 2021

help.why: Rubber gets old and hard, even when the tread still looks fine, especially in the South African sun. Old tyres can crack and come apart. Many tyre makers advise replacing tyres after about 6 years.
howToCheck: Find the code on the side of the tyre that starts with DOT.
The last 4 numbers show when it was made: the week, then the year. 2321 means week 23 of 2021.
Work out how old each tyre is.
help.markMonitor: 5 to 6 years old: plan to replace.
help.markFixNow: Over 6 years old, or cracking.
help.looksLike: On the side of every tyre is a code starting with DOT. The last four numbers in an oval are the week and year it was made: 2321 means week 23 of 2021.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Older than 6 years, even if the tread looks fine.
One tyre much older than the others on the same axle.
Fine cracks between the tread blocks or on the sidewall.

items.hint: Level ground, engine off for a few minutes

help.why: Oil stops the engine’s metal parts grinding against each other. Without enough oil, the engine can be destroyed in minutes, which costs tens of thousands of rands. Milky, creamy oil can mean coolant is leaking into the engine, a sign of a head gasket problem.
help.safetyFirst: Engine off, on level ground, for at least 5 minutes. Parts of the engine can be very hot.
howToCheck: Open the bonnet and pull out the dipstick (usually a yellow or orange loop).
Wipe it clean with a cloth, push it all the way back in, then pull it out again.
The oil mark should be between the two marks (MIN and MAX, or two dots).
Look at the colour: golden-brown is good, black means a service is due, milky means stop and call the workshop.
help.markMonitor: Close to MIN (top up with the right oil), or very black.
help.markFixNow: Below MIN, milky, or the oil warning light came on.
help.looksLike: The dipstick is a long thin metal stick with a coloured loop handle (usually yellow or orange). At its tip are two marks (MIN and MAX, two dots, or a cross-hatched area). Clean oil looks golden-brown, like honey or tea.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The oil mark is near or below the bottom mark.
Overdue for a service.
Looks like coffee with milk: coolant is getting into the oil, a head gasket sign. Don’t drive.
Above the top mark, which can also damage the engine.

help.why: Coolant carries heat away from the engine. If it runs low, the engine overheats, which can ruin the head gasket (the problem KVS has now).
help.safetyFirst: Only check with the engine cold. Never open the radiator cap on a hot engine: boiling water can spray out and burn you.
howToCheck: Find the see-through plastic coolant tank with MIN and MAX marks.
Look at the level from the side, without opening it.
If it’s low, top it up with the correct coolant mix (not plain tap water) and tell the workshop if it keeps dropping.
help.markFixNow: Below MIN or empty, keeps dropping, or the engine overheated.
help.looksLike: A see-through plastic tank with MIN and MAX (or LOW and FULL) marks on its side, connected to the radiator. The liquid inside is coloured: green, pink, blue or orange, depending on the brand.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The level is near or below MIN.
It needs topping up every week: a leak, or a head gasket or cooler problem.
Rusty or oily: a sign of an internal problem.
Bubbling with the engine running: a head gasket sign.

help.why: Brake fluid carries the push from your foot on the pedal to the brakes at the wheels. A low level can mean the brake pads are worn or there’s a leak, and the brakes could fail.
help.safetyFirst: Don’t open the brake fluid cap. Brake fluid damages paint and skin.
howToCheck: Find the small tank at the back of the engine bay on the driver’s side, usually with a yellow cap.
Check the level is between MIN and MAX by looking from the side.
Look at the colour: clear gold is good, dark brown means it’s old.
help.markFixNow: Below MIN: don’t drive, call the workshop.
help.looksLike: A small see-through tank at the back of the engine bay on the driver’s side, usually with a yellow cap and MIN and MAX marks. New fluid is clear and golden, like cooking oil.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Near MIN: brake pads are worn, or there’s a leak.
Brown or black: the fluid is old and needs changing.
Dampness on the tank, the pipes, or the inside of a wheel.

help.why: Power steering fluid makes the steering light and easy to turn. If it runs low, the steering gets heavy and the pump gets damaged. Many newer vehicles have electric steering with no fluid at all: then mark N/A.
howToCheck: Find the power steering tank (its cap often shows a steering wheel).
Check the level against the marks.
help.markFixNow: Very low, or the steering is heavy or whining.
help.looksLike: If the vehicle has hydraulic power steering, there’s a small tank with a cap showing a steering wheel symbol, and MIN and MAX marks. Electric power steering has no tank.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Below MIN.
A howl or whine when you turn the steering wheel while parked.
It’s hard to turn at low speed.

help.why: Without washer fluid you can’t clean a dirty windscreen while driving.
howToCheck: Find the tank with the windscreen symbol on the cap.
Fill it with water and a little windscreen washer liquid. Don’t use dishwashing liquid: it leaves a film.
help.looksLike: A large tank with a cap showing a windscreen spray symbol, usually blue or black.

whatGoesWrong.signs: No spray from the jets.
The tank empties without being used.

help.why: An automatic gearbox needs clean fluid to change gears smoothly. Old or low fluid can ruin the gearbox, one of the most expensive repairs.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Low, burnt or leaking.

help.why: The battery starts the vehicle. Loose or crusty connections are one of the most common reasons a vehicle won’t start.
help.safetyFirst: Never touch both battery terminals with anything metal at the same time: it can spark and burn.
howToCheck: Find the battery and look at the two terminals: + (red) and – (black).
Look for white, green or blue powdery crust.
With gloves on, wiggle each cable. It must not move.
help.markFixNow: A loose cable, or a cracked or swollen battery.
help.looksLike: A black box with two metal posts on top: + (red cover) and – (black). The cable clamps should be tight and the posts clean and shiny. Some batteries have a little window on top that shows green when the battery is healthy.

whatGoesWrong.signs: White, green or blue fluffy powder on the posts.
The cable turns or wiggles on the post.
The sides bulge out, or there’s a crack or wetness.
The engine turns over slowly when you start it.

help.why: A battery can look fine but be weak inside. A battery tester shows how much strength is left, so it can be replaced before it leaves someone stranded.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Failed the test.

items.text: Drive belt: no cracks or squealing

help.why: The drive belt turns the parts that charge the battery, run the aircon and often pump the coolant. If it snaps, the battery goes flat and the engine can overheat.
help.safetyFirst: Engine off and keys out of the ignition. Keep your hands away from the fan.
howToCheck: Find the long rubber belt at the front of the engine.
Look for cracks, frayed edges or shiny, glazed rubber.
When you start the engine, listen: a loud squeal can mean the belt is slipping.
help.markMonitor: Small cracks, or a squeal on cold mornings.
help.markFixNow: Frayed, deep cracks or missing pieces.
help.looksLike: A flat black rubber belt with ridges on one side, running around several round pulleys at the front of the engine.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Small cracks across the ridged side.
Loose threads at the edges.
The surface looks shiny and smooth.
A high squeal when you start the engine or switch on the aircon.

items.text: Radiator and heater hoses: no cracks or leaks

help.why: Rubber hoses carry hot coolant between the engine and the radiator. An old hose can burst and the engine overheats within minutes.
help.safetyFirst: Only touch the hoses with the engine cold.
howToCheck: Look at the big rubber hoses going to the radiator.
Squeeze them (engine cold). They should feel firm, not soft, sticky or rock hard.
Look for cracks, bulges, wet spots, or white or green crust at the ends.
help.markMonitor: Slightly soft or crusty at the clips.
help.markFixNow: Cracked, bulging or leaking.
help.looksLike: Thick black rubber pipes, about as wide as a thumb or wider, running between the engine and the radiator. They’re held on with metal clips.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It feels spongy or has a bulge.
Small cracks, especially near the ends.
Wet patches, or white, green or pink crust at the clips.

help.why: The air filter cleans the air going into the engine. On dusty roads it clogs up, the engine loses power and uses more fuel.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markMonitor: Dirty: replace at the next service.
help.markFixNow: Blocked or damaged.

items.text: No oil or fluid leaks in the engine bay or on the ground
items.hint: Look where the vehicle was parked overnight

help.why: A leak is often the first sign that something is wearing out. Catching it early prevents a breakdown. The colour of the drip tells you what it is.
howToCheck: Look at the ground where the vehicle stood overnight.
Black or brown drips: oil. Green, pink or orange: coolant. Red: gearbox or steering fluid. Clear water under the front is normal: it comes from the aircon.
Look in the engine bay for wet, oily patches.
help.markFixNow: A puddle, or any coolant or brake fluid leak.
help.looksLike: The ground under a parked vehicle should be dry. Clear water dripping under the front, after the aircon has been running, is normal.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Black or brown drops, sticky and slippery.
Green, pink or orange drops that smell sweet.
Red or brown drops.
Clear, slippery drops near a wheel. Don’t drive.
A strong diesel or petrol smell, or a rainbow sheen on wet ground.

items.hint: Rodents nest in engine bays of parked vehicles

help.why: Mice and rats like to nest in the engine bays of parked vehicles and chew the wiring. That can cause electrical faults or even a fire.
howToCheck: Look in the engine bay for nests, droppings, food or chewed plastic.
Look for wires with bare copper showing or hanging loose.
help.markMonitor: Signs of rodents, but no damage yet.
help.markFixNow: Chewed or bare wires.
help.looksLike: Wires are bundled in black plastic tubes and tape, clipped neatly along the engine bay. None should hang loose or show bare metal.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Bare copper or bite marks on the plastic.
Nests of leaves or paper, droppings, or food stashed on top of the engine.
A connector hanging unplugged.

help.why: Rubber mounts hold the engine and gearbox in place and soak up vibration. Broken mounts cause clunks and shaking, and strain other parts.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Broken.

items.text: Timing belt or chain replacement up to date
items.hint: Check the km of the last replacement

help.why: The timing belt or chain keeps the engine’s moving parts in step. If a belt snaps, the engine can be destroyed. It must be replaced at a set km, which is in the service book.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
Check the km of the last replacement in the service book and when the next one is due.
help.markFixNow: Overdue, or no record of a replacement.

items.text: Seat belts at every seat: latch, retract, not frayed

help.why: Seat belts are the most important safety equipment in the vehicle. In a crash, a belt that doesn’t lock or is frayed can fail. Every seat that a passenger sits in needs a belt that works.
howToCheck: For every seat, pull the belt out quickly. It should lock with a jerk.
Let it go. It should roll back in by itself.
Click it into the buckle and pull hard: it must hold. Press the button: it must release.
Look along the whole belt for cuts and fraying.
help.markOk: Every belt locks, latches and rolls back.
help.markMonitor: A belt is slow to roll back in.
help.markFixNow: Any belt that doesn’t lock or latch, or is cut. Nobody sits in that seat until it’s fixed.
help.looksLike: Each belt is a flat woven strap. It should be smooth with even edges, pull out freely, lock with a sharp tug, and roll back by itself. The buckle should click and hold.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Fuzzy edges, cuts, or burn marks.
A sharp tug pulls more belt out instead of locking.
The belt stays slack across the seat.
It won’t click in, or lets go when you pull hard.

items.text: Dashboard warning lights go off after start-up

help.why: Warning lights are the vehicle’s way of saying something is wrong. When you switch on, they all light up for a few seconds as a test, then go off. One that stays on means a problem.
howToCheck: Turn the key to “on” without starting: the lights come on.
Start the engine. Within a few seconds they should all go off.
If any stay on, photograph the dashboard and note which one.
help.markMonitor: A yellow or orange light stays on: get it checked soon.
help.markFixNow: A red light (oil, temperature, brakes, battery) or a flashing engine light: don’t drive.
help.looksLike: When you turn the key to “on”, lots of small symbols light up on the dashboard for a few seconds as a self-test. Once the engine runs, they should all go out. Red means stop; yellow or orange means get it checked soon.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Low oil pressure: switch off straight away.
Engine too hot: stop safely and switch off.
Not charging: the battery will soon go flat.
Low brake fluid or a brake fault. A handbrake that isn’t fully off can also cause it.
An engine fault is stored. If it flashes, there’s a serious misfire: stop.
The glow plugs. It should go out before you start. If it stays on or flashes while driving, there’s an engine fault.

help.why: The horn warns people and animals. It’s also checked at a roadworthy test.
howToCheck: Press the horn briefly. It should be loud and clear.
help.markFixNow: Doesn’t work.
help.looksLike: Pressing the middle of the steering wheel should give a loud, clear sound.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The sound is quiet or croaky.
A fuse or the horn itself has failed.

help.why: Seats must be firmly attached. A loose seat can break off in a crash, and the driver must be able to adjust the seat to reach the pedals properly.
howToCheck: Push and pull each seat. It must not wobble.
Move the driver’s seat forward and back and adjust the backrest. It must lock in place.
For seats that fold or come out (in vans), check the latches lock.
help.markMonitor: A loose cover or a stiff lever.
help.markFixNow: A seat that wobbles or won’t lock.
help.looksLike: Each seat should be bolted firmly to the floor and should not rock. Adjusters (levers or knobs) should move freely and lock.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It rocks or clicks when you push it.
The seat slides on its own, or the backrest won’t lock.
A removable or folding seat won’t lock into its floor mounts.

help.why: Torn seats get worse quickly, look bad to guests, and bring the price down when the vehicle is sold. Stains are easier to clean when they’re fresh.
howToCheck: Look at each seat for tears, holes and stains.
Photograph new damage so you know when it happened and who had the vehicle.
help.markFixNow: Big tears, or broken springs poking through.
help.looksLike: Seat covers should be whole and clean, with no holes or loose stitching.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Food, drink or mud marks.
Splits in the fabric or seams.
A small melted or brown spot.

help.why: In South African summer, a vehicle without aircon can get dangerously hot for passengers, especially children and older people. Weak aircon usually means it needs gas or a service.
howToCheck: Start the engine and set the aircon to cold with the fan on.
After 2 to 3 minutes, the air from the vents should be properly cold.
help.markMonitor: Cool but not cold: book an aircon check.
help.markFixNow: Blows warm, or smells burnt.
help.looksLike: With the engine running, the aircon button on (often a snowflake or “A/C”) and the temperature on cold, the air from the vents should feel properly cold within 2 to 3 minutes.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Low gas or a compressor fault.
The compressor cuts in and out.
A musty smell, from mould in the system.
A rattle or squeal when the aircon starts.

help.why: The demister clears a fogged-up windscreen on cold or rainy mornings. Without it, the driver can’t see.
howToCheck: Once the engine is warm, set the temperature to hot and the air to the windscreen.
Warm air should come out and clear the glass.
help.markFixNow: No warm air, or the windscreen stays fogged.
help.looksLike: With the engine warm, the temperature on hot and the air directed at the windscreen, warm air should clear a misted screen within a few minutes.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Low coolant, or a heater fault.
The air doesn’t reach the windscreen, or the screen fogs up again.
A heater leak inside the dashboard. Get it checked.

help.why: The fan pushes the air through. If some speeds don’t work, a small part (the resistor) usually needs replacing.
howToCheck: Turn the fan through each speed. Each should be stronger than the last.
help.markFixNow: Fan doesn’t work at all.
help.looksLike: The fan control has several speeds. Each step should blow harder than the last.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Only the top speed works: a failed resistor.
A fuse or the fan motor.
Leaves or dirt caught in the fan.

help.why: Gauges tell the driver how fast they’re going, how much fuel is left and whether the engine is too hot. A broken speedometer leads to speeding fines; a broken fuel gauge leads to running out of fuel.
howToCheck: On a drive, check the speedometer and rev counter move.
Check the fuel gauge matches what you expect.
Once the engine is warm, the temperature needle should sit in the middle.
help.markFixNow: Speedometer, fuel or temperature gauge doesn’t work.
help.looksLike: The speedometer shows the speed, the fuel gauge the fuel level, and the temperature needle should sit near the middle once the engine is warm.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The needle doesn’t move, or jumps around.
It shows full after a long trip, or empty after filling up.
The needle climbs above the middle.

help.why: Doors must lock to keep the vehicle and what’s inside it safe.
howToCheck: Lock with the remote. Every door, including the sliding and back doors, should lock and the indicators flash.
Unlock: every door should open.
Also try the key in the driver’s door.
help.markFixNow: A door doesn’t lock.
help.looksLike: Pressing lock on the remote should lock every door, including the sliding doors and the tailgate, and the indicators flash once. Unlock should open them all.

whatGoesWrong.signs: One lock motor has failed. Check each door by pulling the handle.
The remote battery is weak.
A lock motor is failing.

items.text: Interior door handles and child locks

help.why: Passengers must be able to get out quickly in an emergency. Child locks stop children opening the back doors while driving, but must be off when adults travel so they can get out.
howToCheck: Open each door from the inside.
Find the child lock switch on the edge of the back or sliding doors and check it works. Set it the way it’s needed.
help.markFixNow: A door can’t be opened from inside (with the child lock off).
help.looksLike: Every door should open from the inside. The child lock is a small switch or slot on the edge of the back or sliding doors, visible when the door is open.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The child lock is on, or the handle or cable is broken.
It flops without opening the door.

items.text: Floor mats secure and clear of the pedals

help.why: A loose mat can slide forward and jam under the brake or accelerator pedal. This has caused serious accidents.
howToCheck: Check the driver’s mat is clipped in, or lies flat and can’t slide.
Press each pedal all the way down. Nothing should get in the way.
Never put two mats on top of each other.
help.markFixNow: A mat bunches up under the pedals.
help.looksLike: The driver’s mat should lie flat and be held in place by clips or hooks so it can’t slide forward.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It rides up against the pedals.
One mat on top of another can jam the pedals.
The driver’s heel can catch in it.

help.why: Not a safety item, but drivers use it for navigation and hands-free calls, and a working radio shows the vehicle is cared for.
howToCheck: Switch on the radio and check the sound from all speakers.
Test Bluetooth or a phone connection if it has one.
help.markMonitor: A speaker or Bluetooth doesn’t work.
help.markFixNow: (Rarely urgent.)
help.looksLike: The radio should switch on, find stations, and play sound from all speakers.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Fuse, wiring or speaker fault.
A damaged speaker.
Some radios lock after the battery was disconnected and need a code.

help.why: Drivers need to charge phones for navigation and emergencies on long trips.
howToCheck: Plug a phone into each socket. It should start charging.
help.markFixNow: (Rarely urgent.)
help.looksLike: USB ports and 12 V sockets (round, like a cigarette lighter) should charge a phone.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A blown fuse, often from a faulty charger.
The plug falls out or the charging cuts in and out.

items.text: Roof lining, trim and sun visors

help.why: A sagging roof lining or loose trim looks bad, can hang into the driver’s view, and brings the price down when selling. (WeBuyCars noted a sagging roof lining on JYD.) Sun visors must stay where you put them.
howToCheck: Look at the roof lining for sagging.
Look for loose or missing trim pieces.
Fold the sun visors down and up. They should stay put.
help.markMonitor: Some sagging or a loose piece.
help.markFixNow: Lining or trim hanging into the driver’s view.
help.looksLike: The roof lining should be tight against the roof. Trim panels should be clipped in place with no gaps, and sun visors should stay where you put them.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The cloth hangs down in a bubble, usually from the back.
Panels rattle or have come off their clips.
It drops down on its own.

help.why: Guests and teams use these vehicles, so a clean vehicle makes a good first impression. Rubbish attracts rats and mice, and things left behind (phones, documents) need to be returned.
howToCheck: Check under and between the seats and in the door pockets.
Remove rubbish. Keep any lost items safe and report them.
Shake out the mats and wipe the dashboard if it’s dirty.
help.markFixNow: Very dirty, food or rubbish left, or a bad smell.
help.looksLike: A clean cabin has no rubbish, sand or food, and nothing left behind in the seat pockets, door pockets or under the seats.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Wrappers, bottles or crumbs. These attract rodents.
Phones, chargers, clothes or documents.
Spilled food, wet carpets, or smoke.

items.text: Warning triangle, jack and spare wheel in the vehicle

help.why: If a tyre bursts on a trip, the driver needs a working spare, a jack and wheel spanner, and a triangle to warn traffic. Without them, a simple puncture becomes a long and dangerous wait on the side of the road.
howToCheck: Check the warning triangle is in the vehicle.
Check the jack and wheel spanner are there.
Check the spare wheel is there and not flat.
help.markFixNow: Anything missing.
help.looksLike: The warning triangle folds flat in a red case. The jack, the wheel spanner and the spare wheel are in their places.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The bag or slot is empty.
The spare is flat, worn, or the wrong size.

help.why: When the vehicle breaks down on the road, a warning triangle placed well behind it tells other drivers to slow down before they reach you.
howToCheck: Find the triangle (often in the boot or under a seat).
Open it up. It should stand up and the reflectors shouldn’t be broken.
Remember: put it about 45 m behind the vehicle, roughly 60 big steps.
help.markFixNow: Missing.
help.looksLike: A red reflective triangle that folds out and stands on a small base.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Not in the vehicle.
Legs snapped or reflectors cracked.

help.why: If someone gets hurt, the first few minutes matter. A stocked first-aid kit lets you stop bleeding, clean wounds and protect yourself with gloves while waiting for help.
howToCheck: Open the kit.
Check for gloves, bandages, plasters, gauze, antiseptic, scissors and a CPR mouthpiece.
Check expiry dates, and replace anything that was used.
help.markMonitor: A few items missing or expired.
help.markFixNow: No kit, or it’s empty.
help.looksLike: A box or bag marked with a cross. Inside: gloves, bandages of different sizes, plasters, gauze, antiseptic, scissors, a foil blanket and a CPR mouthpiece.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Empty spaces, opened packets.
Dates printed on the packets have passed.
Water damage or a broken seal.

items.text: Fire extinguisher present and in date

help.why: A small fire in the engine bay can be put out early with an extinguisher, before it spreads. An empty or expired one is useless.
howToCheck: Check it’s firmly mounted so it can’t roll around.
Look at the gauge: the needle must be in the green.
Check the service tag date. Extinguishers are usually serviced every year.
help.markOk: Needle in green, service in date.
help.markFixNow: Needle in red, seal broken, or missing.
help.looksLike: A red cylinder held in a bracket, with a small pressure gauge on top. The needle should be in the green zone, the safety pin in place, and the service tag in date.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The needle is in the red zone.
The pin is missing or the seal is broken.
The service tag is more than a year old.
It rolls around: in a crash it becomes a missile.

help.why: Without a jack and wheel spanner, nobody can change a flat tyre.
howToCheck: Find the jack and wheel spanner and check nothing is missing.
Check the spanner fits the wheel nuts, and the locknut key is with it.
help.markFixNow: Missing or broken.
help.looksLike: The jack is a small scissor or bottle jack. The wheel spanner is an L-shaped or straight bar with a socket that fits the wheel nuts. The locknut key sits with them.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The storage space is empty.
It doesn’t fit the wheel nuts.
The screw won’t turn.

help.why: Anyone standing next to the road after a breakdown could be hit. A reflective vest makes them visible from far away, especially at night.
howToCheck: Check there’s at least one vest within reach of the driver, not buried under luggage.
help.markFixNow: Missing.
help.looksLike: A bright yellow or orange vest with silver reflective stripes, kept within reach of the driver.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Not in the vehicle.
The reflective strips no longer shine.

help.why: Breakdowns often happen at night. A torch is needed to look at the engine, change a tyre or signal for help.
howToCheck: Switch it on to check the batteries.
help.markFixNow: Missing or dead.
help.looksLike: A working torch with fresh batteries, stored in the cubby hole or door pocket.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Weak yellow light, or none.
Not in the vehicle.

help.why: In an emergency, the driver needs the right phone numbers fast: the FFSA vehicle coordinator, the insurer and roadside assistance, the tracking company, and emergency services (10111 for police, 112 from a cellphone).
howToCheck: Check the card is in the cubby hole or on the sun visor.
Check it has the vehicle coordinator’s number and the insurer’s claims and roadside-assistance numbers. The insurance and registration papers themselves stay in the legal office.
Check the numbers are current.
help.markFixNow: Missing.
help.looksLike: A card in the cubby hole or on the sun visor with: the FFSA vehicle coordinator’s number, the insurance and roadside-assistance numbers, the tracking company’s number, and emergency numbers (112 from a cellphone, 10111 for police). The registration papers and insurance documents themselves are kept in the legal office.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Not in the vehicle.
A number on the card no longer works, or a person has left.

help.why: An engine that’s slow to start often warns of a weak battery or starter motor before it leaves someone stranded.
help.safetyFirst: Do the road test on a quiet road or in an empty parking area, with your seat belt on.
howToCheck: On a diesel, turn the key to “on” and wait for the coil-shaped glow plug light to go off first.
Start the engine. It should start within a few seconds.
Listen while it idles. It should run smoothly without shaking or stumbling.
help.markMonitor: Slow to start, or rough for the first few seconds.
help.markFixNow: Hard to start, or shakes and misfires.
help.looksLike: A healthy engine starts within about 2 seconds of turning the key and settles to a smooth, even hum.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The engine turns slowly before starting: a weak battery or starter.
On a diesel, often glow plugs, fuel filter or the battery, especially on cold mornings.
The engine shakes, stumbles or the revs hunt up and down.
A loud rattle for a few seconds after starting.

help.why: New noises are early warnings. Knocking can mean engine trouble, whining can mean a worn pump or bearing, and rattling is often a loose heat shield or suspension part.
howToCheck: Drive with the radio off and the windows slightly open.
Listen while you speed up, brake, turn and go over bumps.
Note when the noise happens and where it seems to come from.
help.markFixNow: Knocking, grinding, or a loud whine.
help.looksLike: Normal sounds: a steady engine hum, some tyre noise and wind. Anything new or rhythmic is worth noting.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A deep tapping that speeds up with the engine.
Rises and falls with speed: a bearing, the gearbox or the differential.
Worn suspension parts.
A worn CV joint (front wheels).
A loose heat shield or exhaust.

items.text: No blue, black or white exhaust smoke

help.why: The colour of exhaust smoke is a clue. Blue smoke means the engine is burning oil. Black smoke means too much fuel (common on worn diesels). Thick white smoke that smells sweet can mean coolant is burning, a head gasket sign. Thin white vapour on a cold morning is normal.
howToCheck: Ask someone to watch the exhaust while you start the engine and rev it.
Or watch in the mirror as you pull away.
help.markMonitor: A puff of black smoke when accelerating hard (diesel).
help.markFixNow: Blue smoke, constant black smoke, or thick white smoke.
help.looksLike: With a warm engine, the exhaust should be clear. A little white vapour on a cold morning is normal and disappears once warm.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Too much fuel: dirty air filter, injectors or turbo (common on worn diesels).
The engine is burning oil: worn turbo or engine.

whatGoesWrong.problem: Thick white smoke that smells sweet
whatGoesWrong.signs: Coolant is burning: head gasket or cooler problem. Stop and call the workshop.

items.hint: Automatic: no jerks, slips or delay moving off in D and R

help.why: Jerky or slipping gear changes can mean the gearbox needs a service. Gearbox repairs are very expensive, so catching problems early matters.
howToCheck: Standing still with your foot on the brake, select D, then R. Each should engage within about a second, with no clunk.
Move off in D and in R: it should pull away smoothly.
Drive normally and feel each gear change: smooth, without jerks, delays or the revs jumping.
help.markMonitor: An occasional hard or late change.
help.markFixNow: Slips, bangs into gear, or won’t go into gear.
help.looksLike: In an automatic, the gear changes should feel like a gentle nudge, with the revs dropping smoothly after each change. Pulling away in Drive and Reverse should be smooth.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A jolt when changing gear.
The revs flare up but the vehicle doesn’t speed up.
The engine revs high before changing up.
A pause, then a clunk, when you select D or R.
A gearbox light or message on the dashboard.

help.why: If the vehicle pulls to one side, a tyre may be soft, the wheels may be out of alignment, or a brake may be sticking. It tires the driver and wears tyres quickly.
howToCheck: On a straight, flat road with no traffic, relax your grip on the steering wheel for a moment.
The vehicle should keep going straight.
help.markMonitor: Slight pull: check tyre pressures and book an alignment.
help.markFixNow: Strong pull to one side.
help.looksLike: On a straight, flat road the vehicle should keep going straight if you loosen your grip for a moment.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A soft tyre, wheel alignment, or a sticking brake.
Needs constant small corrections: worn steering parts.

help.why: A shaking steering wheel usually means a wheel is out of balance or a rim is bent. A crooked steering wheel while driving straight means the alignment is out.
howToCheck: Drive at 80 to 100 km/h on a smooth road and feel the steering wheel.
Check the steering wheel is straight when the vehicle drives straight.
help.markMonitor: Slight shake at certain speeds: book wheel balancing.
help.markFixNow: Strong shaking, or loose, wandering steering.
help.looksLike: The steering wheel should be centred when you drive straight and should feel smooth and steady.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Usually at 80 to 110 km/h: a wheel out of balance or a bent rim.
Wheel alignment is out.
Worn steering joints.
Worn suspension or steering parts.

items.text: Brakes stop straight, no grinding or squealing

help.why: Brakes are the most important safety system. Grinding can mean the pads are worn down to the metal, and pulling to one side can make the vehicle swerve in an emergency stop.
howToCheck: On an empty road at about 40 km/h, check behind you, then brake firmly.
The vehicle should stop in a straight line.
Listen for grinding or squealing, and feel for shuddering in the pedal.
help.markFixNow: Grinding, pulling to one side, or poor stopping.
help.looksLike: The vehicle should stop in a straight line, quietly, with the pedal feeling firm and smooth.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A harsh metal-on-metal sound: pads worn right down.
A high squeal: pads worn to the warning tab, or dust and glazing.
A stuck or uneven brake on one side.
Warped brake discs.

help.why: A soft or spongy brake pedal can mean air or a leak in the brake system. The brakes could fail suddenly.
howToCheck: With the engine running and the vehicle standing still, press the brake pedal firmly.
It should feel firm, stop well above the floor, and not slowly sink.
help.markFixNow: Spongy, or sinks towards the floor.
help.looksLike: With the engine running, the brake pedal should go down a short way and then feel firm, well above the floor.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It feels soft, like pressing a sponge: air in the brakes.
It slowly goes towards the floor while you hold it: a leak.
Very hard to press: a brake servo problem.

items.hint: Test it in N (neutral), not P

help.why: The handbrake stops a parked vehicle rolling away, which could hurt someone or cause a crash. On an automatic, P also holds the vehicle, so a weak handbrake can go unnoticed until the day someone parks in N or the P lock fails.
help.safetyFirst: Use a gentle slope with nobody behind the vehicle, and keep your foot ready on the brake.
howToCheck: Stop on a slope with your foot on the brake.
Move the gear lever to N (neutral). Don’t test in P: in P the gearbox holds the vehicle, so you wouldn’t know whether the handbrake works.
Pull up the handbrake (or press the electric parking brake button) and count the clicks.
Gently lift your foot off the brake pedal. The vehicle must not move.
Foot back on the brake, and select P before you get out.
help.markFixNow: Vehicle rolls in N.
help.looksLike: With the gear lever in N and the handbrake on, the vehicle should stay still on a slope. A lever handbrake usually needs 5 to 8 clicks.

whatGoesWrong.signs: The vehicle creeps on a slope.
The lever comes up almost to the top.
The handbrake light stays on after releasing it.

help.why: If the engine gets too hot, it can be badly damaged within minutes. The temperature needle should stay in the middle.
howToCheck: After 10 to 15 minutes of driving, check the temperature needle.
It should sit around the middle, also in slow traffic.
help.markMonitor: Rises a little in traffic, then comes back.
help.markFixNow: Goes above the middle or the warning light comes on: stop safely and switch off.
help.looksLike: The temperature needle rises for the first few minutes, then stays in the middle, even in traffic and up hills.

whatGoesWrong.signs: It moves above the middle, especially in slow traffic or on hills.
No fan sound after the engine stops while hot.
Pull over and switch off.

items.text: ABS and traction lights stay off

help.why: ABS stops the wheels locking in an emergency stop, so the driver can still steer around danger. If its light stays on, ABS may not work when it’s needed.
howToCheck: Watch the ABS and traction-control lights after starting and while driving. They should stay off.
help.markFixNow: ABS or traction light stays on.
help.looksLike: The ABS light (the letters ABS in a circle) and the traction light (a car with wavy lines) should go out after start-up and stay off.

whatGoesWrong.signs: A wheel sensor or ABS fault: normal brakes work, but not the anti-lock.
The traction control system is off or faulty.

help.why: Cruise control helps on long trips, but it must switch off the moment the driver touches the brake.
howToCheck: On an open road, set the cruise control.
Touch the brake. It must switch off immediately.
help.markFixNow: Doesn’t switch off with the brake. Mark N/A if there’s no cruise control.
help.looksLike: Cruise control buttons are on the steering wheel or a stalk. Once set, it should hold the speed, and switch off as soon as you touch the brake.

whatGoesWrong.signs: Nothing happens when you press set.

whatGoesWrong.problem: Doesn’t switch off with the brake
whatGoesWrong.signs: A brake switch fault. Don’t use cruise control until it’s fixed.

help.why: Brake pads squeeze the brake disc to slow the wheel down, a bit like squeezing a spinning bicycle wheel with your hands. Pads wear thinner every time you brake. When they’re too thin, the vehicle takes longer to stop and metal grinds on metal, which ruins the discs.
howToCheck: Workshop check: the mechanic takes the wheel off and measures how much pad is left in mm.
Type in the number from their report.
help.markMonitor: 2 to 4 mm: replace at the next service.
help.markFixNow: Under 2 mm, or the mechanic says replace now.

help.why: Brake pads squeeze the brake disc to slow the wheel down, a bit like squeezing a spinning bicycle wheel with your hands. Pads wear thinner every time you brake. When they’re too thin, the vehicle takes longer to stop and metal grinds on metal, which ruins the discs.
howToCheck: Workshop check: the mechanic takes the wheel off and measures how much pad is left in mm.
Type in the number from their report.
help.markMonitor: 2 to 4 mm: replace at the next service.
help.markFixNow: Under 2 mm, or the mechanic says replace now.

help.why: Brake discs (and drums at the back on some vehicles) are what the pads grab. Worn or warped discs make the steering or pedal shake when braking and reduce stopping power.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markMonitor: Worn: replace with the next pads.
help.markFixNow: Below the limit, cracked or badly warped.

help.why: Brake pipes and hoses carry the brake fluid. A leaking or cracked one can make the brakes fail.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Leaking or badly corroded.

help.why: Shock absorbers stop the vehicle bouncing. Worn ones make it sway, take longer to stop and wear tyres faster, which matters a lot in a full van.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Leaking or broken.

help.why: Rubber bushes and ball joints connect the wheels to the vehicle and let them move. Worn ones cause clunks and poor handling, and a badly worn ball joint can let a wheel collapse.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Excessive play or torn.

items.text: Tie rod ends and steering rack

help.why: Tie rods connect the steering wheel to the front wheels. Worn ones make the steering loose and the vehicle wander.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Loose steering.

help.why: CV joints let the front wheels turn while the engine drives them. If the rubber boot tears, the grease falls out and the joint fails. A clicking sound when turning is the warning sign.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Boot torn, or the joint clicks.

help.why: Wheel bearings let the wheels spin smoothly. A worn bearing hums or growls, and can eventually seize.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Loud noise or play.

help.why: A leaking exhaust can let fumes, including poisonous carbon monoxide, into the cabin. Loose parts can fall off on the road.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Leaking, or loose mountings.

help.why: The gearbox and differential need their oil. A leak that runs them dry causes very expensive damage.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Dripping.

help.why: A fuel leak is a fire risk.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Any fuel leak or smell.

help.why: The chassis is the vehicle’s backbone. Damage or rust through it makes the vehicle unsafe in a crash and fails a roadworthy test.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Damage or rust through the metal.

items.text: Diagnostic scan: no stored fault codes

help.why: A diagnostic computer reads fault codes stored in the vehicle’s computer, even problems that haven’t switched on a warning light yet.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Active fault codes that need repair.

help.why: Wheel alignment makes the wheels point straight. When it’s out, tyres wear on one edge and the vehicle pulls.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Far out, or tyres wearing badly.

help.why: Coolant needs the right mix to protect the engine from rust and overheating. The workshop tests its strength.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Contaminated, or oil in the coolant.

help.why: The aircon needs the right amount of gas to blow cold. Low gas usually means a small leak.
howToCheck: Workshop check: you don’t need to do this yourself. Record what the mechanic’s report says.
help.markFixNow: Empty or leaking.
